what: RXO is one of the largest truck freight brokers in North America. It does not own trucks: it matches shippers’ loads with independent carriers, earning the difference between what shippers pay and what carriers charge. It was spun out of XPO in 2022 and bought Coyote Logistics from UPS in 2024.
customers: Retailers, manufacturers and food companies that need trucks, and the small trucking companies and owner-operators that haul the loads.
money: Arranging full-truck shipments with outside carriers; RXO keeps the spread.
Running freight for large shippers on an outsourced basis, and delivering bulky goods to homes.
moat: Scale and technology in a fragmented market: its software prices and matches loads quickly, and a bigger network of carriers means fewer empty miles. But brokerage has low switching costs, and margins depend on the freight cycle.
risks: The truck freight market has been in a long downturn, with too many carriers and weak rates squeezing broker margins.
RXO has lost money in each of the last two years, $290M in 2024 and $100M in 2025.
Buying Coyote doubled the business but brought integration costs and lower-margin contracts.
Diluted shares rose from 115M to 168M, mostly from the stock sold to pay for Coyote.
opportunities: Revenue of $6.5B over the last twelve months is well above any earlier year, so the combined network is larger.
When the freight cycle turns, brokers with large networks can widen spreads quickly.
Debt of $727M is manageable against $1.5B of equity.
C.H. Robinson has shown that a broker can cut costs sharply with technology; RXO is attempting the same.
watch: Gross margin per load in truckload brokerage, which shows whether the cycle is turning in its favour.
view: RXO is a bet on the end of the freight recession. Brokers make money from the gap between what shippers pay and what truckers accept, and that gap has been squeezed for three years because there are too many trucks chasing too little freight. RXO has lost money in both of its last two years, and the forward P/E of 62 shows that even analysts do not expect much profit next year.

What it has done in the meantime is get bigger. Coyote turned RXO into one of the two or three largest brokers in the country, with $6.5 billion of trailing revenue. Size matters in brokerage when the market tightens, because more loads and more carriers mean better matches and wider spreads. It does not matter much while the market is weak, as the losses show.

The analysts’ average target is only 6% above the price, which fairly reflects the uncertainty. I would not buy RXO for its current numbers. The case is purely cyclical: when truck capacity leaves the market, freight rates and broker margins can jump quickly, and RXO has the most to gain. The risk is that the downturn lasts another year or more, and C.H. Robinson’s faster cost cutting takes share in the meantime.
bull: Truck capacity finally shrinks, broker spreads widen and the larger RXO earns far more than today’s price implies.
bear: The freight recession drags on, Coyote’s integration costs linger and more efficient rivals take share.
